questions.question: Define the normal, angle of incidence and angle of reflection, and state the law of reflection. A ray strikes a mirror at 25° to the surface: what are the angles of incidence and reflection?
questions.expected_answer: The normal is an imaginary line at 90° to the surface at the point of incidence. The angle of incidence is the angle between the incident ray and the normal; the angle of reflection is the angle between the reflected ray and the normal. Law: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane. At 25° to the surface, the angle with the normal is 90° − 25° = 65°, so the angle of incidence is 65° and the angle of reflection is 65°.

questions.question: Describe five properties of the image formed by a plane mirror and explain why the image appears to be behind the mirror.
questions.expected_answer: The image is virtual (cannot be caught on a screen), upright, the same size as the object, the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front, and laterally inverted (left and right swapped). Light from the object reflects off the mirror according to the law of reflection; the reflected rays enter the eye, and the brain traces them back in straight lines to the point they appear to come from, which lies behind the mirror, although no light actually goes there.

questions.question: Distinguish between regular and diffuse reflection, explaining each in terms of the surface and the law of reflection. Why is diffuse reflection important for seeing everyday objects? Give one use of reflection.
questions.expected_answer: Regular (specular) reflection occurs at smooth surfaces (mirror, still water); parallel incident rays meet the surface at the same angle and reflect parallel, forming a clear image. Diffuse reflection occurs at rough surfaces (paper, cloth, walls); the surface is tilted differently at each point, so although every ray obeys the law of reflection, the reflected rays go in many directions and no image forms. Diffuse reflection sends light in all directions, so objects can be seen from anywhere and without glare. Uses: car mirrors, periscopes, retroreflectors on road signs, heliostats, telescope mirrors.
